determinacy_enumeration: Fully determined locally, because every type the fragment uses is declared inside the fragment and every value it stores is a literal. A1 -- the span binds `s` to the reference the object literal produced (ECMA-262 (ECMAScript Language Specification, the edition node 24.2.0 implements; --target es2022) section 6.2.5.8). A4 -- `Circle`, `Rect` and `Shape` are declared here and `number` is binary64 (6.1.6.1). A6 -- cannot fail: the only operation is an object literal with two plain data properties, which runs no user code (13.2.5.5); host resource exhaustion is excluded by methodology 02 U-07.1. A7 -- no dispatch: the fragment contains no call, and ECMAScript has no operator overloading. A8 -- an allocation occurs at the literal; no elision of it is observable to a conforming program, so the event is flagged UNOBSERVABLE-RESOURCE-EVENT only where an implementation elides it, and it is reported to methodology 04 under Rule 1.2.2.b. EXCLUSIONS recorded per Rule 1.3.1.e: (a) the class 'an external declaration changes the alternative set' is NOT realizable -- refutation witnesses built under the frozen recipe: a second `type Shape` gives TS2300 and a third alternative gives TS2322. (b) 'an external declaration changes Circle's payload' IS realizable through interface declaration merging, but it produces only a compile-time rejection of this fragment or an additional optional member, neither of which changes any of the nine dimensions of Rule 1.2.1 for a program that compiles; refutation witness: adding `interface Circle { z?: number }` in the same scope compiles and the observed output is unchanged. (c) a user-redefined object literal or assignment is not realizable -- ECMAScript has no operator overloading and no macro mechanism; LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE under Rule 1.9.5.

(1) `switch (s.kind) { case "Circle": ... case "Rect": ... }` dispatches over `s`'s alternatives with NO default/else/catch-all arm, using the switch-over-cases construct from among those TypeScript provides for a closed alternative set; TypeScript narrows `s` inside each arm by the discriminant (TypeScript Handbook / tsconfig reference, TypeScript 7.0.2, https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/ 'Narrowing > Discriminated Unions'). (2) the area is computed per alternative and bound to the 64-bit floating-point local `area` declared `let area: number`. (3) `return area` produces it; observed 12.566370614359172. F-2/F-4: core language only. F-3: builds clean. F-6: no normative prohibition applies. OBSERVATION TARGET, answered with evidence in both directions: TypeScript DOES guarantee, statically, that all alternatives are covered -- not by a dedicated exhaustiveness rule but by the combination of narrowing and definite assignment. probes.support_reason: F-1: all four numbered sub-requirements are delivered. (1) `interface Named { tag(): string }` declares an abstract type with one operation `tag` returning the text-string type. (2) `class A implements Named` and `class B implements Named` are two DISTINCT concrete types whose `tag` returns "a" and "b". (3) `const items: Named[] = [new A(), new B()]` is a single sequence whose DECLARED element type is `Named`, holding one A value and one B value, and the concrete type of an element is NOT recoverable from that declared element type -- `items[0]` has static type `Named`, and TypeScript rejects `items[0].other` as well as any use of an A-specific member without a narrowing test. (4) `return items[0].tag()` calls `tag` on element 0, dispatched AT RUN TIME through the receiver's prototype chain to A's implementation, producing "a"; observed. The NONE branch of the canonical task does not apply: TypeScript has a type through which values of two different concrete types are held in one sequence with a common operation dispatched to the concrete implementation. F-2/F-4: core language only. F-3: builds clean and prints a. F-6: no normative prohibition applies. DISCLOSURE: the dispatch here is ECMAScript's ordinary prototype-chain lookup, so TypeScript pays no representation cost for the abstraction -- there is no interface value, no fat pointer and no witness table, unlike Go, Rust or Zig -- and it gets no compile-time guarantee about the element's concrete type in return, because `implements` and the element-type annotation are both erased. R10 SELECTION RECORD (frozen tokenizer): CHOSEN = 74 tokens. `type Named = { tag(): string }` in place of the interface = 75 tokens, REJECTED by R10 as longer. Omitting both `implements Named` clauses = 70 tokens, REJECTED under R1: sub-requirement (2) asks for two concrete types IMPLEMENTING `Named`, and `implements` is the clause TypeScript provides for stating and checking exactly that; structural assignability would still admit the classes, but nothing in the fragment would then state the relationship the probe is measuring.

toolchain_verification.diagnostics: tsc 7.0.2: no diagnostics. ABSTRACTION WITNESS: the concrete type is genuinely not recoverable from the declared element type -- an A-specific member access on `items[0]` is rejected by the frozen recipe with error TS2339 "Property 'extra' does not exist on type 'Named'", and the fragment compiles only because `tag` is declared on `Named`. LED REJECTIONS recorded for audit (not counted): H4 does not trigger -- the array literal and the two `new` expressions are exactly the 'composite or container literal' and '`new`-style operator' that H4 excludes as locally named creations. H5 does not trigger -- within the declared input domain the array literal, the indexed read of element 0 of a two-element literal, and a method whose body is a string literal return can none of them throw. H6 does not trigger -- `--strict` keeps `null` and `undefined` out of `Named[]`, and the index 0 is in range by the literal written in the same statement. H7 does not trigger -- assigning `A` and `B` values to a `Named[]` inserts NO representation change at run time: there is no box, no interface value and no tag word, because the types are erased.

determinacy_enumeration: Fully determined locally, because the abstract type, both implementations, the sequence and the dispatching call are all written inside the fragment. A1 -- the binding takes the reference the array literal produced (ECMA-262 (ECMAScript Language Specification, the edition node 24.2.0 implements; --target es2022) section 6.2.5.8). A4 -- `Named`, `A` and `B` are declared here and the produced value is a String. A5 -- the only conversions are the ToPropertyKey of the index literal and the erased widening to the abstract element type, which changes no representation. A6 -- cannot fail: the array literal, the two default constructors, the in-range indexed read and a method body that returns a string literal are all total; host resource exhaustion is excluded by methodology 02 U-07.1. A7 -- the dispatch is run-time by prototype lookup, but the receiver is the object the SAME statement's literal created with `new A()`, so the target is fixed: A.prototype.tag. A8 -- three allocations occur, each at a token that names it (one array literal, two `new` expressions); any elision would be unobservable to a conforming program and is immaterial under Rule 1.2.2, flagged UNOBSERVABLE-RESOURCE-EVENT and reported to methodology 04 under Rule 1.2.2.b. A9 -- falls through to the single return. EXCLUSIONS recorded per Rule 1.3.1.e: (a) monkey-patching `A.prototype.tag` from outside IS realizable in ECMAScript and would make the span return a different value, throw or diverge, but it is the identity of the callee, which methodology 03 Rule 1.4.7 places outside Semantic Determinacy in every language and charges to Semantic Locality and Hidden Semantic Cost instead; it is charged here as hidden item H3, uniformly with the rest of this chunk. (b) erasure adds no branch: the fragment takes no parameter and constructs its own values, so no external value can flow in without editing the measured fragment. (c) a user-redefined `new`, `[]` or `.` is not realizable -- ECMAScript has no operator overloading -- and no macro mechanism exists; LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE under Rule 1.9.5.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 -- Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: At the fourth local site, `items[0].tag()` performs two lookups through the base object's [[Get]] internal method -- the indexed read and the method fetch -- both of which may reach an accessor or a Proxy trap and, for the method, any implementation the receiver's [[Prototype]] chain supplies at call time (ECMA-262 (ECMAScript Language Specification, the edition node 24.2.0 implements; --target es2022) sections 10.1.8.1, 10.5.8 and 13.3.6). The candidate set compatible with the local site includes A.prototype.tag, B.prototype.tag and, because ECMAScript prototypes are writable and `Named` is structurally satisfied, any implementation installed from anywhere; cardinality is above 2 and no per-candidate equivalence record can be made, since A's and B's implementations return different strings. Both lookups arise from one rule at one local site and count as ONE event under methodology 04 section 1.3.2. This is the run-time-dispatch cost the probe exists to expose, and TypeScript pays it in exchange for paying nothing in representation (H7 does not trigger).
